Lutte contre le racisme : 180 M$ engagés: Fighting racism: $180M committed, but what measurable results for Quebec?
Le ministre responsable de la Lutte cont: The minister responsible for the Fight Against Racism, Christopher Skeete, at a press conference. Credit: screenshot from a press conference
Je me suis intéressé au bilan du Groupe: I took an interest in the assessment of the Groupe d’action contre le racisme because it goes straight to La Converse’s core mission: staying close to communities and examining, rigorously, how public decisions concretely affect their daily lives. Five years after the publication of the report Le racisme au Québec : tolérance zéro, it seemed important to me to check what a “100%” announced by the government really means.
Pour préparer ce reportage, j’ai d’abord: To prepare this report, I first compared the 2020 report with the final assessment published in February 2026 in order to measure the gap between the initial commitments and their implementation. I reviewed the 25 actions, analyzed the breakdown of the $180M invested, and sought reactions from the office of the responsible minister, members of the National Assembly, rights advocacy organizations and researchers specializing in public policy. My goal was not to settle the debate, but to clarify the issues of accountability and to make these documents accessible to the general public.
La question du racisme étant sensible et: Because racism is a sensitive and politically polarized issue, I took care to report what each person said faithfully and to clearly distinguish verifiable facts from the analyses offered by the people interviewed.
<strong>À l’automne 2020, la mort, filmé: In the fall of 2020, the death of Joyce Echaquan at the Joliette hospital, filmed live, sent a shockwave through Quebec. A few months later, amid international mobilizations against racism and heated political debates over the recognition of systemic racism, the government presented an action plan titled Le racisme au Québec : tolérance zéro. Five years and $180M invested later, the government says that 100% of the 25 actions have been carried out or are on their way to being completed.
<strong>Mais dans un climat toujours pol: But in a climate that remains polarized, marked notably by the adoption of the Act respecting the laicity of the State and by recurring controversies in the National Assembly, several community and legal stakeholders dispute the real scope of this assessment, which they consider more administrative than anything. In their view, it does not allow us to adequately measure whether progress has been made on the ground.
Le<l1> document</l1> publié en février 2: The<l1> document</l1> published in February 2026 highlights several measures, including guidelines against arbitrary police stops, data collection on police interventions, awareness campaigns in schools, improved equal access to employment and the creation of housing for Indigenous students.
Dans ce bilan, Christopher Skeete, minis: In this assessment, Christopher Skeete, the minister responsible for the Fight Against Racism, says he is “satisfied with and grateful for the diligence with which the ministries and agencies involved implemented the 25 actions recommended by the Groupe d’action contre le racisme (GACR).” The working group, created in June 2020, had presented its <l1>recommendations</l1> six months later. The ministry says it now sees “very concrete results from this collective mobilization. […] these efforts are advancing the fight against racism and helping build a fairer, more inclusive and more united Quebec.”
Néanmoins, plusieurs voix dénoncent un d: Nevertheless, several voices denounce a gap between the government’s accounting and the realities lived on the ground. For several measures, it is hard to judge whether they have had concrete, measurable effects. For example, have police stops deemed discriminatory decreased? Has access to employment or housing improved?
Pour reprendre une analogie simple, on p: To use a simple analogy, a hospital can announce that it has put a new protocol in place, trained its staff and bought equipment, but are patients getting better care day to day?
Interrogé sur cet écart entre outils et: Asked about this gap between tools and measurable effects, the ministry, through its communications department, says it is “acting with the tools at our disposal, and that means laws and action plans.” It cites in particular a governance scholarship program, increased representation of visible minorities on the boards of directors of Crown corporations, awareness campaigns in sports and improved access to Indigenous-language interpreters to facilitate access to justice.
Le bilan fait état de plus de 180 M$ inv: The assessment reports more than $180M invested over four years by the various ministries and agencies that contributed to implementing the GACR action plan.
Ainsi, 36,45 M$ ont été investis afin de: For example, $36.45M was invested to provide adult learners and Indigenous students with culturally adapted housing in Sept-Îles, Trois-Rivières and Québec City, so that access to housing is not an additional worry during their studies.
Cyrille Ekwalla, directeur de l’Institut: Cyrille Ekwalla, director of the Institut NéoQuébec, questions how the money was actually distributed. “It’s not the amount that impresses me. It’s rather: what did you allocate that amount to? As someone who experiences discrimination, I don’t see these 180 million.”
Au terme de l’examen des dépenses détail: After reviewing the detailed spending for the past four years, obtained by La Converse, one finding stands out: $100M (about 55% of the total budget) went to a single measure, namely the recognition of immigrants’ credentials.
À ce stade, ces démarches ont mené à la: At this stage, these efforts have led to the signing of an agreement with Switzerland and to talks with five other countries. Bridging programs, among other things to facilitate the recognition of skills, have also helped speed up the process. The assessment reports that more than 1,300 people “settled, with their family members, in every region of Quebec, in order to complete bridging training or a clinical internship and then be hired in the health network as nurses.”
Rappelons que l’ancien ministre responsa: It should be recalled that the former minister responsible for the Fight Against Racism, Benoit Charette, had pointed out at a <l1>press briefing</l1> in December 2021 that the recognition of prior learning was a major component of the plan and “probably the most important” for “making sure we don’t waste potential.” A few days earlier, Jean Boulet, then Minister of Labour and Immigration, had presented <l2>a plan for the recognition</l2> of immigrants’ skills, with a budget of $130M. Those funds now count among the investments tallied in the anti-racism plan.
Interrogé à ce sujet, Maxim Fortin, cher: Asked about this, Maxim Fortin, a researcher at the Institut de recherche et d’informations socioéconomiques (IRIS), sees “something telling” in it. For him, “it reflects how the government perceives the problem.” Even though, in his view, the fight against racism “is not a problem in terms of the amount of money put on the table, but a qualitative problem,” Mr. Fortin considers that the emphasis on labour market integration reflects the Coalition avenir Québec’s tendency to read the fight against racism mainly in economic terms. “They sidestep the question of rights deprivation by betting on functional integration,” he adds.
<strong>Lutte contre le racisme : une fo: Fighting racism: a symbolic ministerial role with no real portfolio
« Le gouvernement doit être exemplaire d: “The government must lead by example in the fight against racism, using the levers it has directly at its disposal.” So states the GACR Action Plan. Among its recommendations is the appointment of a minister responsible for the Fight Against Racism, in order to increase accountability for the results of the actions implemented.
Si un ministre siège désormais au Consei: While a minister now sits in cabinet with this mandate, there is no ministry with an autonomous budget comparable to other portfolios. Responsibility instead rests with a Bureau de la lutte contre le racisme, tasked with coordinating the actions of 11 ministries and agencies.
Selon les données transmises à La Conver: According to data provided to La Converse by the ministry’s communications branch, the funds dedicated to the Bureau rose from about $400,000 in 2021-2022 to $649,100 in 2025-2026. These amounts mainly cover operating costs and the pay of a coordinator and a few strategic advisers.
À titre comparatif, le bilan gouvernemen: By comparison, the government’s assessment reports more than $180M invested under the plan, spread across different ministries. The Bureau does not manage them directly, but handles monitoring and coordination. This structure raises a question of accountability: who bears responsibility for the results if the objectives are not met?
Pour Andrés Fontecilla, député de Québec: For Andrés Fontecilla, a Québec solidaire member of the National Assembly, this setup can be justified since racism cuts across several fields of action. But “by giving the mandate to verify progress with few resources, one can question the political will,” he says.
Le ministère répond que le Bureau dispos: The ministry responds that the Bureau has “a team dedicated specifically to follow-ups with ministries and agencies,” in addition to managing certain initiatives such as the introduction of mandatory training on racism for state employees and the<l1> Prix pour un Québec sans racisme</l1>.
Safa Chebbi pousse la critique plus loin: Safa Chebbi takes the criticism further. According to the coordinator of the Observatoire des inégalités raciales du Québec, creating a junior ministry without a substantial budget or clear decision-making power can amount to symbolic stagecraft.
La première des 25 actions concerne les: The first of the 25 actions concerns police stops and racial profiling. On this point, the criticism is blunt. For Lynda Khelil, policy file officer at the Ligue des droits et libertés (LDL), the assessment confirms a refusal to tackle the problem at its root. “The Quebec government does not take the problem of racial profiling seriously at all,” she says. “It’s linked to the fact that it refuses to recognize that racism is a systemic phenomenon.”
Le ministère réplique en disant avoir po: The ministry counters that it has taken “concrete action on several fronts,” notably by adopting guidelines governing police stops, adding social workers alongside police forces and enhancing continuing education. “Many of these measures have already borne fruit and will continue to do so over the long term,” it says.
La réponse du ministre ne comporte pas d: The minister’s response includes no example of these “fruits”; on top of that, no independent conclusion on a decline in profiling is included in the assessment.

Dans le document gouvernemental, une int: In the government document, a police stop is presented as “an activity
permettant aux policiers d’accomplir adé: that allows police officers to do their job properly.” For the Ligue, this framing implicitly legitimizes the practice of stops, which, unlike arrests, fall within an area of broad police discretion.
Le gouvernement affirme avoir renforcé l: The government says it has strengthened protections against housing discrimination, improved equal access to employment and increased training for state agents. Yet, according to several stakeholders, the measures remain largely informational or educational. “We see a lot of training-based actions,” observes Safa Chebbi. But, she adds, “training doesn’t solve the problem at its core.”
Elle estime que le racisme est souvent t: She believes racism is often treated as an individual phenomenon, citing the example of the “cop who behaves badly,” rather than as a set of institutional biases.
Cyrille Ekwalla abonde dans le même sens: Cyrille Ekwalla agrees. “Why aren’t acts of discrimination more clearly punishable? Why not move toward stronger legislative changes?” he asks.
Sur la question du logement, le ministèr: On housing, the ministry maintains that “all legislative tools are in place” and urges citizens to turn to the Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse to obtain justice. Québec solidaire MNA Andrés Fontecilla counters that the government “could go further” than simply informing tenants about recourses for discrimination, notably by applying more binding measures.
Le débat s’inscrit dans un contexte poli: The debate takes place in a broader political context. The Coalition avenir Québec, in power since 2018, refuses to recognize the existence of systemic racism or the <l1>Joyce’s Principle</l1>.
Pour les organisations consultées, cette: For the organizations consulted, this position influences the nature of the measures adopted. “If you don’t recognize that racism is systemic, you’re going to propose cosmetic measures,” says Lynda Khelil.
Cinq ans après « Tolérance zéro », le go: Five years after “Tolérance zéro,” the government presents an administrative apparatus in motion: guidelines, training, campaigns, committed budgets. The progress is sometimes quantified. As of October 30, 2025, the representation rate of visible minority members across the public service was 16.1%, equivalent to 96.9% of the 2028 target.
Les critiques ne nient pas l’existence d: The critics do not deny that this progress exists. “We can’t throw everything in the trash,” acknowledges Safa Chebbi. “There are steps forward.” But the fight against racism cannot be reduced to a series of tallied actions. “The need is even greater than before,” says Cyrille Ekwalla, pointing to an international context marked by identity-based withdrawal and the normalization of certain discourses.
Maintenant que le gouvernement a établi: Now that the government has drawn up its final assessment, the question remains: has Quebec transformed its institutions, or has it mainly documented its efforts?
